correctness.rationale: For each fixed center the candidate averaging rows are all different. Outside the resulting finite set of tie hyperplanes the maximizing rows form a strict branch. A segment with positive generic endpoints has only finitely many switches; summing the variation bounds on its linear pieces, then using continuity to approximate arbitrary nonnegative endpoints, bounds the global two-input quotient by the maximum strict-branch norm. Conversely a small perturbation of a strictly feasible, positively translated baseline realizes its branch on both inputs. The linear branch preserves constants; integration of binary upper-level cuts gives exact cyclic coarea for the input and a triangle-inequality bound for the output. Its norm is therefore the maximum over all proper nonempty cuts, including disconnected ones. Independent exact enumeration gives the unrestricted envelopes 1, 5/4, 7/5, 2 and exactly three C₆ masks above 19/10. In each exceptional mask the two full rows are opposite; their competing radius-one triples partition the cycle, so the full average is the mean of the two triple averages and cannot strictly exceed both. Thus the only excessive masks are not strict branches. The four displayed baseline and cut perturbation pairs were checked to retain their unique branches and attain the claimed constants; for C₆ their variation pair is 1/50 and 19/500.
residual_risks: The finite mask lemma is exhaustive only for the specified sizes; extension to all real nonnegative input pairs uses the branch and cut arguments, not sampling. No bound is claimed for the absolute-value maximal operator on arbitrary signed inputs.

value.rationale: The sizes are a meaningful cutoff rather than an arbitrary sample: the unrestricted row envelope is sharp for the first three cycles and first fails at C₆, where opposed full-cycle choices create a new feasibility constraint. The exact modulus quantifies sensitivity to differences between two signals, a question not answered by one-input variation bounds. The cut reduction and analytic obstruction explain why exhaustive small-instance values are sharp and why the naive bound first overestimates them.
residual_risks: No assertion for larger or weighted cycles, other ball conventions, or other seminorms.
